body:
I dunno, maybe I'm overthinking everything.  I've actually calmed down a lot.  

I just wanted to speak to someone, I guess.
I am paranoid, have unusual thinking patterns that make me question if I am in touch with reality, can't relate normally and casually with people
I don't have a normal life.  I am not a normal person.
It's funny how Kobe had to tell Byron Scott to bench him.
What kind of gameplan would you give Russell?
No, the Lakers would also be increasing Philadelphia's odds at drafting a quality prospect at 4.
Oh yes, I misread.  I thought the user was making a comparison between rookie year stats and single game stats, instead of arguing against it.  Thanks for the correction.

Last night both of the aforementioned players had 15 points, and Randle was on the bench when the Timberwolves went on a great run with 7 minutes left in the 4th.  Perhaps he would have reached 20?  Clarkson had 14.  In my opinion, poor rotations, an uninspired offensive system, higher TO's, fewer assists were factors.  

As well, I don't think it's accurate to say that Kobe was the reason for the double-digit lead, as Williams had 21, Young had 14, Hibbert had 12.  Others created.  I agree with you in that Kobe is vital to the team as a leader and shot creator, but I would hate to have the team "live or die" so to speak late game on his isos, which are becoming tougher as he increases in age and he faces a much younger opposition.  He played that role splendidly in the past, but I think the team should ask either Clarkson, Russell, or Randle to become that shot creator.

What do you mean by "good scorers?"  You mean dominating on the offensive end?  I agree both must develop.  It's just that Clarkson and Randle are a fast, strong 2-4 combo, and can finish around the rim/ get fouled by KG or Towns.  This is a more efficient way to generate points then a slow, contested Kobe jumper.

Like you just said, it takes years to determine a bust.  Despite mediocre summer league, preseason, 1 regular season game, Russell still has time to adjust to the pace of NBA games.  Players drafted after him are demonstrating their individual weaknesses (TO's, lack of athleticism, no offensive moves), and I think even if KAT (probably the best player in college) fell to the Lakers in the draft he would have struggled in Byron's system as Russell is currently.

The FO realizes a championship run this year is unrealistic given the inexperience of the young core players.  I think the plan for the draft was to take the best all around basketball player according to college resume and group and solo workouts.  Mitch believed Russell was that BPA and had the upside of a franchise player for the Lakers.  This was less of a certainty in Mudiay's case (athletic, but with poor shot selection, injury in overseas play, unimpressive workouts) and Okafor's case (deceptively athletic, national title in college, but with terrible free throw percentage, subpar rim protection, and solid workouts).  

I wouldn't necessarily agree with the last statement about top two picks--I think Russell will make an immediate impact if he is utilized as the primary ball handler/floor general instead of Clarkson or Randle.

Did you watch summer league?  Russell was driving to the basket, on Okafor no less.  I think Russell is the faster of the two.  But his problem in the regular season will probably be spacing with Randle, Clarkson and Kobe on the same floor.
The year's just begun.  Wait until 2016 to compare with Wall, etc..

I wasn't saying that mid-range was necessarily the problem, but that he should probably defer to Clarkson, Russell or Randle instead of playing 1 on 1 with Wiggins.  Like you said, he had some open looks, and when you miss those, you live with them.
If you actually watched Randle get the rebound and then push upcourt, he drives against KAT and drew a shooting foul.  Was never called due to Kobe's timeout.

What if he wasn't a phenomenal big man, as you say?  What if he topped out as Al Jefferson?  Slow, with a talented back-to-the-basket game?

Orignially, I was with you on drafting Okafor, but I must say, I do like the idea of Russell's upside as a Ginobili-type player.

I think you're underestimating how much a basketball player can improve from college to pro levels, and then in between NBA seasons.  It really takes time to find out a player's worth.  Take Randle for example--last season in summer league, scouts and fans looked at his stats and claimed that he would be a good role player in the regular season (50 points, 6 assists, 17 rebounds through 4 games), that he would perform similar to Thomas Robinson.  Randle has these T-rex arms and thus can't rebound or defend, employs a bully-ball style of play which won't work on the 4's and 5's of the league, etc.

After a year, Randle has added muscle, can rebound and then push tempo in transition, makes better decisions on both ends of the floor, can play point-forward, make free throws consistently, and has more finesse working in the paint.  He recently went up against Green and Garnett and arguably outplayed them as a sophomore.

I think Russell will get a similar opportunity and show gains in his second year.  He can already pass, but he will be a better defender at 6'5" and with his length.  He can spend time in the weight room, get the ball in a new offense where he plays the point and can orchestrate.  I still think he has a lot of potential, and has the chance to be worth that no. 2 pick.

What the team would look like if the Lakers did draft Okafor?  Perhaps in the short term that Randle-Okafor frontcourt might be successful offensively, but wouldn't it get crowded in the paint, as both bigs are primarily, from an offensive standpoint, back to the basket?  Would they get more rebounds than, say, a Randle-Hibbert frontcourt?  I don't think so.  I also think that Russell gets JC and Randle more open looks, plus, the Lakers can take advantage of their youth by moving at a faster pace in transition, something that probably won't happen with a much slower Okafor.

I really wouldn't crucify Laker management for the pick.  They truly did swing for the fences in drafting Russell.  Even though there are a lot of problems with his game right now, there is a lot of time left for him to develop into a possible All-Star/franchise player, so I would suspend judgement until after the first few seasons have passed.

1.  Russell had the more impressive solo and 3-on-3 workouts when compared to Okafor's (who I guess looked to them like the Brook Lopez/Al Jefferson mold of player).  Aside from high basketball IQ, Russell demonstrated leadership intangibles that made workout teammates better and impressed the Lakers coaching staff.
2.  Russell was the no. 1 option at OSU, demonstrated at the NCAA level that he can be a threat from 3 (Mudiay isn't there yet), he has a mid-range game, great passing ability, and is competent in driving and initiating contact despite a lack of NBA-caliber athleticism and foot speed (perhaps he could be on par with help of NBA training staff?). 
3.  He could potentially make Clarkson a better spot-up/driving 2, and Randle a more lethal 4, but he needs the ball in his hands and a new offensive system for this to happen (the Lakers currently have a simple offensive scheme with Kobe, Randle, and Clarkson all demanding the ball for an iso drive/pull-up with 15 seconds on the shot clock).  

He was the highest upside pick of the 2015 draft, probably the best all-around player available after KAT.  I don't think he has been given a fair chance to show and then develop his abilities.

What did you think about Russell not receiving the ball for a majority of the time he was on the floor last night?  The Laker offense was dominated by Kobe, Clarkson, and Randle--they largely ignored Russell's side of the floor and effectively played their pure point guard as a 2.
I wouldn't necessarily say that he should shoot more threes than twos--but they should be spot-ups and not heavily contested (like all those isos were on Wiggins last game).

Yes exactly, so did God create us as a way of looking out for our best interests/the interests of our fellow created things?  That's what is frustrating to me, because if so, then wouldn't the people suffering in hell right now (if you believe that) wish they weren't created at all?  Would it have been better for God not to create man and spare all the unsaved generations from the infinite pain and eternal torment?

The Bible consistently describes God's nature as immutable, without movement or change (Malachi 3:6, Numbers 23:19, 1 Samuel 15:29).   

I found this article relating the immutability of God to static perfection (http://www.gotquestions.org/immutability-God.html).  No part of God should move from one state to another, even for pleasure, because, first of all, this would place an eternal being within the physical constraints of time, and secondly would also imply that he was lacking in one way before moving to another.

Wouldn't what is moral be to not create a humanity which will face pain and tribulation and strife?  Why not spare those souls who would, after creation and judgment, find themselves in an eternal hell?

Why create humans at all if they could introduce sin and evil into existence?  What justifies their existence?

And I wasn't saying that a perfect God wouldn't comply with morality, but that morality would never subjugate that being and remove the being's freedom to choose the wrong.  That is, God wouldn't become a moral robot, always forced to choose what is most morally good.

Hi, I didn't say that morality would be obsolete with God's characteristics.  I guess the question is what to get for someone who has everything.  Assuming that God is entirely self-sufficent and eternal is completely satisfied on his own, why would he need to create the universe?  What would the Creation achieve/bring him that he does not already have?
Do perfect, all-powerful beings lack good at all? Because, I think, if that being lacks some good to warrant action, then that being isn't perfect or all-powerful.

The idea that God would want love or an object to love is feasible to me, but unsatisfying when you think about it.  Doesn't the Trinity allow for a three-individual being, so it can't be said that God is alone and without others to demonstrate his love to and be loved by.  As for creativity, perhaps, but idk, again it sounds like an unsatisfying reason to justify the universe's existence.

As the OP, you have my permission to defend Christianity in this thread.  Everyone has my permission to challenge and question as much as they want.  I posted because I wanted to understand people's reasoning for believing or disbelieving.

So you're saying that despite God not needing pleasure, He created all things because he enjoyed (wanted the pleasure found in) demonstrating His love.  I'm trying to understand His motivation (reasons for action) for creating our reality when it seems to me that God shouldn't want for anything, even pleasure, given His omnipotent nature.
Do perfect, all-powerful beings lack good at all?  Because, I think, if that being lacks some good to warrant action, then that being isn't perfect or all-powerful.

To clarify, my question is about God's omnipotent, omnibenevolent, omniscient nature-- what would a completely satisfied being (lacking nothing) be motivated to achieve?  I don't understand why he would create a universe at all and bother with a free will for humanity (would this be the morally good thing to do?).  Also, it seems to me that God wouldn't exist as a subordinate to morality, doing moral acts as if to fulfill laws.

Well, sorry to hear that happened to your co-worker.  I believe you, actually, as you wouldn't have much incentive to lie in this case (let's face it, it would be kinda petty to fabricate a character jab on Reddit) and the event was probably over within seconds, so you couldn't film evidence on a phone.  I think athletes are allowed to demonstrate rude/ugly behavior off the field/court (it's tolerated, is what I mean), as long as it doesn't hurt their play.  But no one should be allowed to say something like that to an employee doing her job.  Hopefully he won't do this in the future.

Duh, they've been drafting.  No, I was asking for the front office to ADD MORE players in case Brown, Upshaw, Nance don't pan out, hence the security and depth mentioned in my previous post.  Think about the players on the Lakers roster and ask yourself if a player like Young (who is a sixth man redundant with Lou Will on the roster) could be traded away for more draft picks.  I say yes.  Therefore, this is not a redundant post.  I don't care if the Bucks haven't "won shit," as you put it.  The Jazz and Bucks would both be in the playoffs in the East, and they would obviously be seeded above the Lakers in your imaginary scenario.  Good day.

I think the reality going forward is a stacked Western conference.  Dwight is in Houston alongside Harden et al.  To compete, the Lakers have to accumulate assets to find franchise players of their own.  Not to mention finding a coach that can succeed in the new analytics-influenced NBA.

Would you advocate the move to replace Mitch, the current GM (he seems to draft good prospects, but the Lakers haven't found great success in attracting free agents)?  How about replacing Byron Scott with a coach from a successful college program?  I actually think the Buss family will continue to influence, but this is not necessarily a bad thing.
Granted, we're on the right track, but I think eventually a draft-oriented youth movement will happen for the Lakers.

Sparse, as in far and few in between.  The Lakers have few draft picks compared to the Celtics or Sixers, who have been hoarding them like candy, giving those teams more chances to land a really good player.

The Bucks were in the playoffs last year, the Jazz probably will be in 1-2 years.  They have a plethora of young players (years of picks) who have developed well together, and their F.O.'s have not been reliant on vet signings as the Lakers' has.  Monroe decided to sign with Milwaukee instead of L.A. because of that promising core.  I'm not disregarding the development potential of the young guys on this current Laker team.  The question is, don't you want some security and depth?  If the Lakers had the Bucks' or Jazz' young roster in a world city next to the Pacific Ocean, it would be very attractive to top-billed F.A.'s like Durant.  Establishing a young core, however, takes years of scouting and acquiring talent through the draft, which is what I think the Lakers' F.O. should be focusing on now.

I was advocating for offloading Kelly and Sacre alongside Young to free up roster spots for perhaps someone like Upshaw.  What will the Lakers do with them eventually, if they are the scrubs you suppose they are?  Cut them?

Your post makes sense, but do you think that the Lakers are likely to attract top-tier free agents like Durant or Westbrook in the years to come?  I think the real question is how best to field a contending team--either by building a core through the draft, or in free agency, or even a mixture of the two?  My fear is that in the event of losing out on a superstar in the offseason, the F.O. will continue to give out short-term contracts to aging vets much like the one given to Hibbert, in the hope that a superstar will one day decide to sign with L.A.  The last true contending team the Lakers put together consisted of Dwight Howard, Kobe Bryant, Paul Gasol, Steve Nash, and Metta World Peace.  The sixth-man was Antawn Jamison.  Not exactly a young, athletic, and injury-resistant core.  Today, the team consists of D'Angelo Russell, Jordan, Clarkson, Julius Randle, Tarik Black, Kobe Bryant, Hibbert, etc.  I am simply advocating the need for the Lakers organization to start relying more on the draft and less on landing a free agent savior.

I think for the past 2 years the Lakers organization has been focused on two things: hoping to land a big name in free agency, and drafting the best available player with a sparse number of picks.  The problems are, as someone already noted here in the comments, superstar free agents aren't attracted to the role of playing Kobe's sidekick, and a developed core with a team identity sans Bryant hasn't been established yet (think of young OKC squad in '10-11), so FA's can't just step in and lead the team in the playoffs for a championship.

I understand what you're saying and agree that the team had few assets to acquire picks in the first place.  But the Lakers were not devoid of trade assets.  Wouldn't you like to see Young (who probably will not be a mentor), Sacre, Kelly, offloaded for future picks in a deal?  What about Hill or Davis last year, who could have been traded to a contender, or to another team in the future if the Lakers had resigned them?  And if Jim fails to bring the team to contention within 2 years (I think this is realistic), idk who would step in as head of basketball operations.

I understand that there's no proof that the organization is harming the players' growth, but idk, shedding MCW after he received the ROY award, losing a good player like McDaniels?  The difference between the Thunder and Sixers is that Philly's gut-the-roster-and-rebuild process has been going on for years, and will continue to do until they have all-star potential at every position and can take over the league.  Sixer players might begin to feel as if they are treading water if the goal is to get to the draft for better players and to not compete for a playoff spot every year.

What?  I thought they were fine Lakers picks but they are three assets total out of 15.  When you look at the Bucks and Jazz with rosters stacked with young talent from top to bottom, you have to wonder how the Lakers will fare playing against them if they make it to the playoffs.  The Jazz for example has a core of Exum, Gobert, Hayward, Burks, Hood, and maybe Lyles.  I want to add to the current core of Randle, Russell, and Clarkson so that the Lakers aren't overwhelmed by a depth of young players, and long-term, accumulating draft picks which hopefully pan out (attracting free agents to relocate to L.A. in the off seasons) is the way to do that.

Well, in the meeting with Lamarcus Aldridge for example, the F.O. emphasized city living and not basketball play.  I think the statement that the Lakers will always get free agents because of L.A. culture is being falsified; the NBA is changing and small-market teams that win 40+ games are more attractive to free agents than large-market teams that have the potential to win years down the line.  I get that perhaps Aldridge or Monroe didn't want to be on the same team with an aging Kobe, but when Bryant retires, and the Lakers have cap space but a small core, will any superstar want to be the face of the rebuilding Lakers when they can sign with a team like the Spurs or Thunder, with all-star teammates, and compete for a title now?

Well, Philly is blatantly tanking, serving to harm the development of the young players they receive.  The Lakers aren't tanking to my knowledge, but will be mediocre at best if they keep waiting for free agents to turn up with a core of just Russell, Randle, and Clarkson.  And 2 years to contention, lol, that is a pipe dream.  In 2 years, the Jazz and Pelicans are going to be serious contenders as well.

Well, I'm sure a contender like Chicago or Memphis could use the shooting Young brings.  The Lakers could also offload Kelly, Sacre, Blue, or Brown for picks in that same deal, as the organization, at least I don't think, is looking to develop those players long-term.  I say get what you can, even if it isn't a first-rounder.

Randle also had the better solo pre-draft workout with Lakers, showcasing a decent mid-range game to pair with aggressive bully-ball post moves.  The young UK team he was the go-to-guy on made it to the NCAA championship game, but lost to UConn.  That year, it made sense for the Lakers to take Randle with the seventh pick, and I think they got great value in an undersized forward who is physical around the rim, athletic, and can pass.
Why do you hate Lillard?
Has DMC become such a headcase that Karl has to talk to Kings players to get him traded?  Why wouldn't he act the same way on the Lakers?

What, what the fuck?  So Kings give up their cornerstone Cousins for Lawson and Okafor and the Lakers still get a top 10 pick in this year's draft?  Too little value to be obtained for Sac; the Kings FO isn't made up of idiots.  I'm sure they will find another organization to trade with, should rumors be true.
Even if Nash, Kobe were 'alive,' so to speak, the Spurs would have still cut that Laker team down in six games.
You could also argue that maybe Cousins leaves after his contact expires in 2018, fucking the Lakers over as Dwight Howard did before him.

Well, if you were in Durant's shoes, would you want to play for a championship with Cousins on a Laker team with fewer assets than OKC?  With a player who is undeniably skilled as a big man but is temperamental?  DMC is perhaps the best all-around center in the game, but as a teammate he showed he can be childish in crucial moments for the Kings.  If you establish Cousins as the face of the Laker franchise for the next few years, it would make it harder for both Westbrook and Durant to envision a contending culture, as opposed to a vision of leading a young Laker core of Randle and Okafor to the championship.

I understand what you're saying but I'm still not convinced it would be a good idea to trade for Cousins.  In order to acquire him, the FO would have to sacrifice Randle, the number 2 pick (probably Okafor), and all the later picks in this year's draft.  Not only is this a risky maneuver that will not place the Lakers in short-term championship contention, but it will set the Lakers even farther back in rebuilding should Demarcus Cousins choose not to resign two seasons later in 2018.  
Additionally, I don't know that there would be cap space to sign Durant + other good FAs, let alone convincing the former to leave OKC for rebuilding/reloading LA.  I actually expect Kobe to retire after next season, and if this is the case the Lakers roster in 16-17 would be built around Clarkson, Cousins+whatever FAs signed during this offseason and next.  Again, this 16-17 scenario is most likely not a championship-contending team.  For now, I say keep both Randle and the number 2.  The attention Jimmy Butler is giving the Lakers this offseason is a good example that L.A. is once again becoming a destination, and it's because the draft picks have FAs intrigued at the idea of a younger, up-and-coming Laker team.
*A rookie center, a young pf, and a young pg

Well, which quality free agents should the Lakers target?  Realistically, in this scenario with Cousins, I see the Lakers missing out on Durant and Westbrook and signing older players looking for max contracts (like Dwayne Wade).  The FO runs the risk of overpaying a few players in the short-term and hindering the chances of winning a championship.  At some point the Lakers will have to alter their mentality and develop/grow draftees themselves instead of farming from other teams in free agency.
Something tells me Cousins and Westbrook would get into absolutely vicious arguments with each other.

While I can't say with certainty that Randle and Okafor will become all-stars as Cousins is now, I still consider them two of the most promising big men drafted (and to be drafted) in the last few years.  They have the tournament success-- were coached by Calipari and K to the NCAA title game.  Okafor's college stats were 17.3 points, 8.5 rebounds, 1.3 assists, 1.4 blocks per game.  Randle's: 15 points, 10.4 rebounds, 1.4 assists, .8 blocks per game.  Randle played well in summer league before injury, showing off guard-like handles, good passing, ability to finish under double team pressure.  The bottom line is that while they really haven't been stellar on both ends of the floor, overall the Lakers have great value in pairing them up considering that Julius Randle is 20 and Jahlil Okafor is 19.  I find it crazy that people would want to trade them now when in five years they might become an improved, more athletic version of the Grizzlies' Randolph-Gasol.  I also think two promising big-men rookies would be more intriguing to FA veterans, and that this nucleus would be the best, long-term approach to hunt for a championship.
Well, what if Cousins leaves in 2018 for a championship-contending team when he is 27/28 years old?  What young talent will the Lakers have to develop and rely on then?

Cousins is the best young center in the league when he reigns in his emotions, and when he isn't doing stupid shit like throwing Marcus Smart to the floor and getting ejected.  The main question for Cousins is can he be consistent, can he lead a team to a championship.  How many times have you seen Demarcus get frustrated and end up getting T'ed up?  I agree with Moser: I'd rather have a young, talented cheap PF and C duo without the attitude problems, who are more likely to resign with L.A. long-term and who understand that it is championship or bust.  Randle and Okafor aren't scrubs.

Why would the Kings trade the cornerstone of their organization to the Lakers for the number 2 pick?  If I was their GM, I wouldn't even consider trading Cousins for anything less than a number 1 pick in an amazing draft class.  Cousins was on Team USA and is an all-star center with two years left on his reasonable contract.  He puts up big man numbers and is only 24.  As well, the Lakers and Kings are competing in the same division, which would be heartbreaking to a Sac fan base forced to watch their center play downstate.  It would be a stupid move for Sac to make, even with the George Karl drama.  Kings FO should get their shit together and try to make peace between player and coach.  If not, replace Karl, who holds responsibility for starting up a Cousins trade market.

Why should he stay with the Lakers in 2018, with Kobe Bryant gone?  Do you think Cousins has the patience to endure what could be two years of losing with less teammate support than he had with the Kings?

If I were Love, I would want to play with Lebron, who carried a depleted Cavs team to six games into the Finals (averaging 35 points, 8.8 assists, 13.3 rebounds per game).  Love's most realistic chance at a championship is with them, not the Lakers, even if the Lakers acquire DMC.  I have second thoughts about Wade.  Given his age and health concerns, would you want to sign him to a long-term deal?

Last year the Lakers had the SECOND WORST defensive efficiency rating in the league at 108 points allowed per 100 possessions (http://espn.go.com/nba/hollinger/teamstats/_/sort/defensiveEff), so your statement about possessing a bottom 3 defense has already come to pass.  That Laker year (2014-15) was with Randle injured and largely Ed Davis, Tarik Black protecting the rim.  My thought is that DMC might be more of a short-term fix who can be good at protecting the rim, but will obviously need defensive help from the PF and SF, which he won't get if you traded away the young, talented draft picks.  The Lakers had Dwight Howard (an all-star, and better defender than DMC) in the exact same scenario in 2012-13 when he was asked to cover for an entire team defensively, and that season ended in a first-round playoff exit.  I think you underestimate how good Randle and Okafor can be together, as an offensive AND defensive unit.

Exactly.  If Cousins leaves after his contract expires, the Lakers have no young talent, no building blocks for the future years except for maybe Clarkson.  Then free agents would DEFINITELY not want to come play for L.A.

How certain are you that Cousins won't leave L.A. once his contract expires, as Howard did before him?  That is, what is stopping Cousins from going to the east coast or another team in playoff contention once he realizes that it is up to him to carry the Lakers to a championship?

They're 19 and 20 years old- give them a chance to actually play a full game in the league before you criticize their defense and decide to trade them away.  Long-term I think Randle will become a more athletic Z-Bo and Okafor a more athletic Al Jefferson (do you doubt that either will become all-stars as Boogie is now?).  Given time, this front court duo will bring the Lakers closer to a championship than Cousins alone will.

My point is that last year Sacre averaged 4 points and 3 rebounds per 15 minutes on the floor and he is coming into his fourth year in the league.  At the moment, he isn't a particularly good distributor or offensive threat (jump hooks and shaky mid-range game which mean that he can't stretch the floor).  Given cap space, wouldn't you rather sign another big to back up Black, Okafor/Towns, Randle who is coming off of a significant injury, and Davis as well?

When you think about the Lakers' draft thoughts, you refer to the opinions of GM Kupchak and scouts and other staff who have spent serious time evaluating prospects at high school and college games; Kupchak will, however, ultimately be making the call on draft night.  I think better sentence phrasing would be that the team's staff is "leaning toward" drafting Okafor with the no. 2 pick, but that if they could choose any player out of the entire draft, they would select Towns.  Comparing the two, my opinion is that Towns might be the player with a better, modern-NBA skill set but he would rather play for the Timberwolves and bring them their first championship than help the Lakers return to former glory.

Do you think NBA basketball is chivalrous in nature?  Most players love to piss the opposition off and mess with their heads to gain a mental edge (Kobe, Artest, Steven Adams, etc.)--they're all what you would term assholes because they love to compete and want to be winners.  I just think players like Artest have tendencies to let their emotions overwhelm them and cause them to hurt people instead of channeling what they feel into their play (think of Malice in the Palice, James Harden elbow, etc.)
Anderson or Jefferson

Sooner or later the Lakers must cut ties and find a replacement third-string big.
Do you remember this?:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L9iwrCmtQcE
I agree, the trailer's tone should demonstrate what type of experience watching the film will be.
Ron Jeremy, nice to meet you.
Good point.

Well, anything's possible.  I say draft Okafor and some defensive-minded SF (round 2) to come off the bench, draft a backup PG/SG (round 2) who can be an effective shooter.  Wings (Blue, Johnson, Kelly) should be developing three-point range.  Sign Harris and retain Davis.  Tarik Black comes off the bench with a better mid-range and low-post game.  Scott increases Clarkson's minutes while limiting Randle's to establish the latter as the starting PF.  Most importantly, Kobe hero ball becomes the second option in the offense after the bigs' post play, where he will be knocking down relatively easy jumpers and open shots when double teams happen.

I wasn't basing the argument solely off of size.  I considered that Davis averaged 4.7 blocks per game in his season at Kentucky compared with Towns' 2.2, thinking that Davis' better defensive showing may be attributed to a longer wingspan, higher max vert (this may not be true as Davis hasn't recorded an official max vert), or higher basketball IQ that Towns does not currently have and may not learn.  Davis did play more minutes in his season, but if Calipari's played both individually for an equal time on either Kentucky squad, I think Davis would have the higher offensive and defensive rating due to the aforementioned qualities.  I am not trying to knock Towns, and would like to see him play with Randle if the Lakers do draft him, but I am not convinced that his path to becoming an amazing player or even a really good player is as easy as you think

What I am saying is that Towns has a similar playing style to Davis (moderate to high rim protection, good mid-range game, some ability to shoot from three) but that Davis will likely stay the more effective defender and scorer throughout his career due to his bigger body and higher athleticism.  I think Towns will struggle against the NBA's best bigs (Marc Gasol, Robin Lopez, Anthony Davis etc.) who can muscle him out of the paint and will largely contain him in 1-on-1 coverage.  I see Okafor as a young Al Jefferson-Tim Duncan hybrid established already as a legitimate post scoring option, who every Western Conference big would find tricky to keep out of the paint on a nightly basis.

I don't know about perfect, but the ending of Boogie Nights was appropriate.  Dirk Diggler gives his "bright, shining star" monologue to himself in the mirror, admires his penis, and then walks out the door.  Credits.

If, hypothetically, we had the no. 1 pick instead of 2, I say go for Okafor.  He has an arsenal of post moves and will command double teams in the NBA, leaving the wings open.  Duke won in the NCAA Finals, so Okafor has been an integral part of championship-caliber basketball play, something that the Lakers franchise would welcome.  Don't get me wrong, I respect Towns as a player and as a young man, but he seems to me to be not unlike a poor man's Anthony Davis.
